  "chapter_body_excerpt": "“Danxi said…” The textual life of medical ideas on madness, 1360-1530 Danxi said that dian belongs to Yin and kuang to Yang, that dian is excessive joy and kuang excessive anger. He also stated that the doubling of Yin is dian and the doubling of Yang is kuang. 丹溪謂癲屬陰 狂屬陽 癲多喜 狂多怒 又云重陰者癲 重陽者狂 Xu Chunfu 徐春甫 in Gujin yitong daquan 古今醫統大全 (1556) $ ^{1} $ Chapters 3 and 4 traced a momentous transformation in the etiology of madness from Wind to internal Fire and mucus between the twelfth and the fourteenth century. The Ming dynasty (1368-1644) was not a period of strong epistemological breaks in medicine, but one in which physicians re-orchestrated earlier approaches to form new doctrinal and therapeutic emphases. Xu Chunfu above was citing the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法, a composite work compiled and printed in his own Huizhou Prefecture (Anhui) in the early 1480s and that quickly became the most influential work attributed to Zhu Zhenheng 朱震亨 (\"Danxi\" 丹溪: 1282-1358). This and the next chapter show how the development of Ming medical thinking on dian and kuang was shaped by three important trends that are well symbolized by Xu's quotation: the rising influence of precepts attributed to Danxi, the importance of Huizhou as a center of medical theorizing and publication, and the profound intertextuality of the elite medical tradition. ### 5.1 Intertextual composition and the Danxi corpus The “Danxi corpus” in the history of medical thinking on madness The rise to prominence of a body of teachings attributed to Zhu Zhenheng deeply shaped Ming medical thinking and practice. Zhu's teachings appeared in a wide array of texts books and manuscripts by Zhu, notes by his disciples, works attributed to Zhu that were collated after his death by people who had known him, and later anthologies base ..."

matched_examples.anchor_excerpt: Yongwen mubiao”蔣公用文墓表 [1424], in Yang's Dongli wenji 東里文集 [1440] 16.20b-22b. 71 Yang's preface to Yuji weiji 玉機微義 ended by praising Chen Yi for diffusing medical teachings, as medicine was “the art by which the sages display benevolence upon the people” (醫者聖人仁民之術也; LiuChYQ: 73). History of the Ming (138: 4137) indicates that in the early Zhengtong reign (in or soon after 1436), Yang “dispatched military and civil officials to zhenfu Jiangxi, Huguang, Henan, and Shandong” (分遣文武鎮撫江西湖廣 河南 山東). Yang was probably the one who sent Chen to Shaanxi in 1435. John Dardess (1996: 179-89) discussed Yang's patronizing of natives of Taihe, but said little about his relations with other court officials. 72 LiuChYQ: 463. In 1438 Yang Shiqi had been named Junior Preceptor (少師), a prestige title ranked 1b. Duxian 都憲 is not listed in Hucker 1985, but it probably referred to a post in the Censorate. A sample mistake in Chen's edition: “Wang Andao” 王安道 (Zhu's disciple Wang Liu) was turned into “Yu'an daoren” 玉安道人 (“Taoist master Yu'an”; juan 1, “Wind strokes,” “neiyin si zhongfeng lun” 内因似中風論; LiuChYQ: 117A). 73 Angela Leung (2003b: 132) postulated that Yang's writing a preface for it showed that the Yijing xianxue 醫經小學 was “an important introductory textbook during the early Ming,” but it appears that Yang's preface enabled rather than recognized the influence of this text.
